Wrong. Read the cards. I think both cards explicitly answer the question
asked.

Ex Nihilo
Necromancy
1 blood
+1 stealth action
<nec> Put this card ON THIS VAMPIRE. The vampire with this card gets +1
stealth. Damage inflicted by this vampire in combat is reduced to zero, and
this vampire is immune to non-aggravated damage. This vampire cannot gain
blood; any blood this vampire gains goes to the blood bank instead. During
your master phase, this vampire burns 1 blood or is burned. You may choose
to burn this card during your untap phase.
<NEC> As above, but you may burn this card during any Methuselah's untap
phase

======================

Akhenaten, The Sun Pharoah
4 pool
Unique Mummy with 3 life, 3 strength, 1 bleed.
Akhenaten may play cards requiring basic Necromancy AS A VAMPIRE with a
capacity of 3. ANY COST IN BLOOD IS PAID WITH HIS LIFE. If a card would give
him blood, give hime life. If he is burned, shuffle him into your library.
If he is in combat with a Follower of Set, any damage he inflicts is
aggravated. Akhenaten can burn himself to burn a Follower of Set controlled
by your prey as a (D) action.

=====================

Akky is able to play Ex Nihilo the same way he can play *any* Necromancy
cards--at basic level as if he were a vampire.

Note that while he would normally be able to gain life by gaining blood, in
this case he could *not* gain blood due to explicit limitations in the card
text of Ex Nihilo.

Similarly, the cost he would normally pay in blood is costing him life as
per the card text of Ex Nihilo.

So, he *could* play Ex Nihilo, but it would not necessarily be a great idea.

Cheers,

And in the 'V:TES Official Clarifications, Rulings, and Errata' page under "Allies"
(meaning it applies to all allies), it says, "Ignore all 'burn blood' effects
entirely." The cost-in-blood thing is talking about a minion playing cards or
paying for a voluntary effect on a permanent (e.g. to remove Slaughtering the
Herd at superior) that list a cost to to play the card or use the effect, not
a mandatory thing. Now, you might have an argument that it applies because it's
worded as, "Do this to avoid this", which would make sense to to convert "burn
blood" to "pay life". But I can't find any rules or rulings on that issue, myself.

> A bit unsure whether he canNot gain life under ExN.

Clearly not. At least, not from "gain blood" effects being interpreted as "gain
life".

Fred

How is the meaning of a word "supported" or "unsupported" "by card text"?
Card text does not define a term. Dictionaries define terms. Rules
define terms. Card text does not define terms. Therefore any assumptions
about what any term means are automatically "unsupported by card text",
whether ultimately correct or incorrect.

I acknowledge the definition of "play" and its distinction from the term
"use" in VtES rules. I simply claim it's somewhat counterintuitive. Thus,
a person can read the text of Akhenaten "literally" and still mistakenly
presume it could use the abilities of Ex Nihilo at superior. Reading that
text literally vs. non-literally (figuratively? - whatever that entail) is
not the issue. It's understanding that the definition of "play" has an
unexpected meaning in this context.

By the way, 1.6.2.1 is a clue that "play" and "use" mean different things
but not a definitive one. For instance, some games might refer to "building
a fort" (or some structure or a railroad or whatever) which occurs over a
period of time. Yet the rules also might refer to, "the turn it is built" - in
this case the final turn of building instead of the initial turn. By the
same token, these rules might have a concept of "playing a card" taking place
over multiple turns yet still refer to the "turn the card is played", being
the initial one.

could differing priorities placed on different issues, such as rules
consistency vs. completeness vs. brevity vs. self-evident clarity vs. a number

completeness pieces strike me as being handled incredibly well. It's very
hard to find anything he doesn't have a ready answer for and a line of
reasoning by which he arrived at the answer and by which we, too, could have

principals to being with.

sending people to Internet to need an answer to begin with. This issue and
the independents-with-votes thing are just a couple of items hitting me
lately that seem like they didn't need to be discussed ad nasuem in this
newsgroup but are spawning long threads. In the past, I've noticed at times
different things in the game I couldn't intuitively figure out the answer to
and went running to the rulings page (and/or poured over relevant sections of
the current rules when appropriate) and found no answers. They always do have
answers and when I find out what they are, I discover some principal I guess
I'm expected to have understood beforehand but didn't.

to fix wherever possible and practical.

Normally, such things can be done with:

- a THOROUGH reading of the rules book. No offence to you or anyone
else, but we all know just how often questions are asked which are
covered in some detail in the rulebook. A lot of people have a basic
grasp of the rules, but have never sat down and properly read the
rulebook. I'd commend it to anyone with some spare time e.g. going on
a bus/train ride with not a lot else to do. Being able to cite isn't
necessary, of course, but knowing what's in there and being able to
think "Oh yeah, that rule on when I get a contested card back......"
and be able to flick through it quickly.

- the rulings and online card text files (or another source of the most
up to date card text)

- a fair ability to know "Oh yes, there's a similar set of wording on
<X>. How's that handled?" This one works because of the consistency
you cite. Again, this doesn't require an encyclopaedia, just a
familiarity with them so you can double check for yourself. I find
this one quite valuable when judging/rulemongering. Being able to
turn to a player and saying "Okay, this works like this. It's fairly
simple to remember when you know that <Y> works like that too." It
provides a useful explanation and in-built memory aid.

- the ability to turn off "common sense" when applying such things.
Remember, what you think is common sense and what the man on the
Clapham Ombinus thinks is common sense can be different. So, once you
have the rules and wording down, you need to just apply them
literally, so far as you can, such that you're consistent.

When I can get some design ideas, I'll probably actually devote some
time to a web-site. (My major problem is *always* design.)

On that note, would a fully annotated rulesbook be of use to anyone?
Take the current rulesbook, cite it (as on Lasombra's site etc.) but
stopping for explanations, memory aids, useful points to bear in mind,
examples of what this means with detailed play examples and so on?
Possibly helpful for newbies. Anyone?

a permanent which can be played at inferior or superior (e.g. Raven with one life

The difference seems abundantly clear to me. An out-of-turn card has very explicit
rules about when it can be played, as does an action card as does an action modifier,
reaction, and combat cards. I believe all of these can become permanents by card
text on some card or another (Life Boon, The Embrace, Spying Mission, Cardinal Sin:
Failure of Mission, respectively). Once in play, the card text on these cards now
governs the use of the card, not the rules about how the particular type of card
enters play. There's nothing anywhere in the rules, however, that directly address
or even remotely suggest that having minion X "play a card as a Y" (some other type
of minion than what X is) only works while putting the card in play and NOT afterward
when the card is in play. However much you'd like to portray this point as being
obvious, it simply isn't. It's strange. It's a bit surreal. In any event, it's

it, either. The definition in M-W seems to imply that "playing" has to involve
taking a card out of a player's hand and placing it on the table. As opposed to
drawing it or pulling it out of the deck and putting it on the table. Beyond that,
it doesn't say much. Nor should it.

doesn't involve playing a scoring combination or part of a trick, what we're
doing with Ex Nihilo isn't really "playing" it (according to M-W) anyway. Unless
you accept Scott's incredibly loose definition of "scoring combination". It would
be very inconsistent to be tight as a drum on the definition of "play" and then
turn around and claim Ex Nihilo is a "scoring combination".

My conclusion is that "to play a card" is specifically defined in each game. And
if that definition is at all controversial or if certain fine distinctions (such
as in the card text of Akhenaten) are going to turn on it, then the definition
should be made explicit.

I think that there are two distinct issues here, and you're somehow confusing
the two together.

The first issue is the one dealing with disciplines. With discipline-requiring
cards, you need the discipline to play it. But you don't necessarily need the
discipline to use it (transferring Animalism retainers, etc.). Both Akhenaton
and Ian Forestal have special abilities that let them play Necromancy cards.

The second issue is the distinction between an ally and a vampire. An ally is
not a vampire and thus can not *use* cards requiring a vampire. All your
arguments concerning Ian fail because of the fact that Ian *is* a vampire. That
is why Ian (with his special) can use Ex Nihilo (not just play it) and why
Akhenaton can only play it (and not use it).

together. So which of the two (or both) do you have the problem with?

points that I think Mr. Coupe and LSJ have made. Namely that allies aren't
suffering any of the penalties either (ignore burn blood effects, etc). And how
about the point that since they actually have "capacity" when playing cards,
then according to your argument, Akhenaten can't gain more than 3 life (since
the excess would drain off)? Allies can't pick and choose which benefits they
can use and which penalties they can ignore. Although I was also initially a
bit annoyed Talaq couldn't use Rutor's Hand, not only do I now understand it,
but I definitely agree with it. It is *not* counter-intuitive and, if anything,
the proposals you have suggested are IMHO counter-intuitive or at the very
least quite convoluted.
